title: Natural Light and Productivity: Analyzing the Impacts of Daylighting on Students' and Workers' Health and Alertness
review_question: To comprehensively review recent work exploring the relationship between daylight and students' and workers' health and performance, with a focus on the influence of morning sunlight on circadian system, brain activity, and alertness.

findings.consequent: Workers' and students' health, satisfaction, attention, and performance
findings.quote: We believe that workers' and students' health, satisfaction, attention, and consequently performance are improved with the help of natural light.

findings.consequent: Circadian system, brain activity, and alertness (students)
findings.quote: the influence of morning sunlight on circadian system, brain activity and alertness of students are discussed.

findings.consequent: Generation of Vitamin D through skin, human health
findings.quote: daylight has in terms of its spectral qualities such as in the generation of Vitamin D through our skin.

findings.consequent: Vitamin D production, calcium absorption, bone strength
findings.quote: natural light interacts with our skin through photosynthesis and produces vitamin D. Vitamin D facilitates calcium absorption which strengthens our bones.

findings.consequent: Circadian clock synchronization, blood circulation, metabolism, hormone levels
findings.quote: daylight is essential in synchronizing our circadian clock, which in turns is essential for stimulating blood circulation, influencing our metabolism, and controlling the levels of many of our hormones.

findings.consequent: Health, well-being, alertness, sleep quality, cognitive performance (attention, executive functions, memory)
findings.quote: Studies have also demonstrated that light influences health, well-being, alertness, and sleep quality.

findings.consequent: Sleep quality (building occupants, office workers, students)
findings.quote: All of these studies show that the exposure to natural light improves the sleep quality of building occupants including office workers and students.

findings.consequent: Delayed sleep timing, depression, anxiety, fatigue, reduced circadian cycle, chronic fatigue, other illnesses (via melatonin disruption)
findings.quote: Inadequate exposure to daylight reduces the circadian cycle [16]. As a result, melatonin is secreted at the wrong times of the day causing chronic fatigue, depression, and possibly other illnesses.

findings.consequent: Mood, morale, fatigue, eyestrain
findings.quote: Daylighting has been associated with improved mood, with an enhancement of morale, lower fatigue, and reduced eyestrain.

findings.consequent: Depression (Seasonal Affective Disorder - SAD)
findings.quote: The seasonal depression, usually found among people living in northern latitudes, is referred to as Seasonal Affective Disorder (SAD) which describes the depression caused by lack of daylight.

findings.consequent: Mental performance, aggressive behavior, depression
findings.quote: many studies indicate that daylighting enhances mental performance and decreases aggressive behavior as well as depression.

findings.consequent: Subjective mood (office workers)
findings.quote: varying lighting levels have a potential advantage for office workers as far as their subjective mood.

findings.consequent: Connection to nature, mood (building occupants)
findings.quote: Daylighting can enhance a connection to nature and directly improve the mood of the building occupants.

findings.consequent: Vitamin D
findings.quote: Physically: Improve Vitamin D

findings.consequent: Cancer possibility, abnormal bone formation
findings.quote: Physically: Decrease Cancer Possibility, Abnormal Bone Formation

findings.consequent: Visual system, circadian rhythms, sleep quality, mood, mental performance, alertness, brain activity
findings.quote: Psychologically: Improve Mood, Mental Performance, Alertness, Brain activity

findings.consequent: Depression, stress, sadness, violent behavior
findings.quote: Psychologically: Decrease Depression, Stress, Sadness, Violent Behavior

findings.antecedent: Daylighting/lighting conditions (via visual, circadian, and perceptual systems)
findings.consequent: Productivity/performance (individuals)
findings.quote: lighting conditions can affect the performance of individuals: (1) visual system, (2) circadian system, (3) and perceptual system.

findings.consequent: Attention during work hours
findings.quote: people with views of natural vegetation posed more attention during the work hours.

findings.consequent: Attention and alertness (during post-lunch dip, for mundane/repetitive tasks)
findings.quote: Natural light increases attention and alertness during the post-lunch dip and was shown to be helpful in increasing alertness for mundane and repetitive tasks.

findings.antecedent: New building with window views (daylighting) + personal control over workstation environmental attributes
findings.consequent: Claims processing productivity (employees)
findings.quote: employees had a 16% increase in claims processing productivity in the new building.

findings.consequent: Visual acceptance scores, sleepiness, physical well-being, visual comfort, alertness, work satisfaction, productivity
findings.quote: Higher visual comfort, alertness, and well-being can be one of the indicators of office workers work satisfaction and all of these factors enhance productivity as a result.

findings.consequent: Vitality, physical activity, sleep quality, sleep duration (office workers)
findings.quote: office workers with plenty of daylight throughout the day sleep on average 46 minutes longer than their counterparts with no daylight and windows.

findings.consequent: Absenteeism
findings.quote: Studies focused on absenteeism as a gauge to measure productivity.

findings.consequent: Physical and emotional health (students and teachers)
findings.quote: Applying adequate daylighting techniques into the architecture of a school contributes the occupants' physical and emotional health.

findings.consequent: Student attendance, health, academic performance, stress
findings.quote: Saving energy, high student attendance, good health and strong academic performance, and a less stress for students are only a few benefits of adequate daylighting in educational environments.

findings.consequent: Happiness (teachers)
findings.quote: teachers are happier when they have the ability to control their environment.

findings.consequent: Eyestrain, information processing, learning ability, stress levels (students)
findings.quote: Poor light spectral quality in the classroom can create a strain on students' eyes, lead to a decrease in information processing and in learning ability and may cause higher stress levels in students.

findings.consequent: Cortisol pattern, stress, children's health, concentration
findings.quote: work in classrooms without windows affected the basic pattern of the hormone cortisol, which is related to stress, and could, therefore, have a negative effect on children's health and concentration.

findings.consequent: Behavior, circadian hormone levels (elementary students)
findings.quote: observed behavior and circadian hormone levels of elementary students in classrooms with natural light stayed closer to expected norms in comparison with students in classrooms with only fluorescent lighting.

findings.consequent: Student test scores (math, reading)
findings.quote: addition of natural light improves student test scores by up to 20%.

findings.consequent: Educational environment quality, learning performance (students)
findings.quote: daylight had an influence on the quality of the educational environment, and students' learning performance.

findings.consequent: MVPA (Moderate and Vigorous Physical Activity), sedentary time, physical activity, vitality, performance (young students)
findings.quote: average light exposure is positively associated with time in MVPA and negatively associated with sedentary time.

findings.antecedent: Full spectrum fluorescent lights or natural light (vs. traditional fluorescent)
findings.consequent: Student and teacher attendance, faculty health absences
findings.quote: students had an attendance increase of 3.2 to 3.8 more days per year than students in traditional fluorescent lighting schools.

findings.consequent: Brain functions, responses, visual/non-visual effects
findings.quote: visual and non-visual effects of light on brain functions and responses are dependent on the specific wavelength of the light received through the eye.

findings.antecedent: Morning sunlight (short wavelength) vs. afternoon sunlight (long wavelength)
findings.consequent: Human body/brain
findings.quote: morning sunlight with a short wavelength spectrum influences people's body differently compared to the long wavelength of afternoon sunlight.

findings.antecedent: Blue light (460nm) exposure during biological night (vs. green light 555nm)
findings.consequent: Subjective sleepiness, auditory performance, alertness
findings.quote: 6.5 hours exposure to blue light (460-nm monochromatic light) during the biological night decreases subjective sleepiness and enhances auditory performance and alertness compared with exposure to an equal photon density of green light.

findings.consequent: Alerting impacts
findings.quote: alerting impacts of ocular light exposure are wavelength dependent and there is a greater sensitivity to short wavelengths in the visible spectrum.

findings.antecedent: Blue light exposure (short duration) vs. green light
findings.consequent: Brain activity (left hippocampus, left thalamus, right amygdala)
findings.quote: 50 seconds exposure to blue light increases activity in the left hippocampus, left thalamus, and right amygdala, as compared to green light.

findings.consequent: Metabolic rhythms synchronization, circadian clock synchronization
findings.quote: Morning light plays an essential role in the synchronization of metabolic rhythms to the 24h rotational cycle of the Earth.

synthesis_conclusions: Daylighting significantly influences human health, well-being, alertness, and cognitive performance in both workers and students.
Natural light, particularly its spectral qualities and dynamic nature, is crucial for synchronizing circadian rhythms, which in turn affects sleep quality, mood, and cognitive functions.
Exposure to natural light, especially in the morning, can improve academic performance, reduce absenteeism, and enhance productivity in educational and office settings.
The non-visual effects of light, mediated by specific photoreceptors and wavelength-dependent brain responses, play a critical role in these positive outcomes.
Access to natural views and personal control over environmental attributes further enhance the benefits of daylighting on productivity and well-being.
evidence_gaps: Research on the impact of natural light on students has been somewhat scarce.
